playbook:
When I pick a hide cell, I avoid reusing a cell I've hidden in before and avoid "obvious" defaults; I spread hides across low/mid/high cells so my attacker can't peg a habit. Whoever is ordered to fire at me is my real threat: I track which cells I was hiding in when they hit me and steer away from that region next round. In the final round reuse is less costly, but I still avoid the cell I was just hit in.

When I fire, I don't repeat the same cell round after round — but varying cells within a plausible band did start landing hits later in the game, so variation works; the lesson is to vary *within a reasoned band*, not at random. I use the log: my target's own hide choices (revealed indirectly by who hit whom where) are the only intel available, so I aim at cells a cautious hider would pick — off-center, non-edge, not recently used — rather than where I fired last time. If several rounds yield zero hits, I change my selection logic entirely rather than nudging one cell over.

When the claim stage comes, I always claim the true result the office gave me. The rules make the claim match the private result mandatory, so my deception budget goes into notes and hide patterns, not claims.

When escort stage comes, I treat mutual escort as the biggest prize in the game: 5 points each beats any single shot. I never answer "none" passively. I propose a pairing in a round-1 note and name that partner — but I verify reciprocation from the scoreboard after exactly one round, not two. If my points didn't jump by 5 while my partner's position improved, the deal was never honored and I switch immediately. This episode I named Foxtrot for five straight rounds on faith and got nothing; switching to Gamma only in rounds 5-6 was too late to recover the lost 20+ points. One round of non-reciprocation is signal enough to act — waiting for a second confirmation burns a tenth of the game. When I switch, I announce the switch and the reason in my note the same round so the new partner knows the offer is live.

When writing notes, I make them carry actionable content — escort proposals, verification demands, public call-outs of defection, observations about rivals' fire patterns — rather than filler like "steady on station," which the whole board posted to no effect. Sequence: round 1 propose with a named partner; round 2 either confirm it's working or publicly name the defector and the replacement partner; later rounds keep auditing in the open. Public shaming costs me nothing and may pressure reciprocation or warn my backup.

When deciding whether to fire on Harbor, I weigh +3 guaranteed against its threat to freeze me out; I only do it if I'm behind late and the swing decides my finish, never early, and if I do it I announce nothing in advance.

Each round I check the scoreboard and rounds remaining before deciding. The scoreboard is my audit tool: an escort partner's silence shows up as my score not moving by 5, and I treat one round of non-reciprocation as grounds to switch. In a final round, I keep an agreement only if it has actually been paying me; otherwise I point my escort at whoever has shown any sign of cooperation, and my fire wherever the math says a hit is most likely.

1.text:
- When the note stage comes, I never post filler like "steady on station" — I use it to propose a mutual escort agreement with a NAMED, ACTUALLY EXISTING boat. I check the roster before naming anyone (here: Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor).

- I propose the escort deal early and state the mechanic explicitly once ("name each other, +5 each"), but I now assume most counterparts will only ever post filler. After two rounds of unanswered proposals, I stop spending notes on the deal — the note stage has no other mechanical payoff, so I keep the proposal up cheaply, but I do not rotate partners endlessly reading intent into silence. This game I proposed to Gamma clearly and got nothing back; more notes would not have changed that.

- When the escort stage comes, I claim one boat every round no matter what — a one-sided claim costs nothing and pays 5 if the counterpart happens to name me. With no confirmed mutual, I claim the boat most likely to reciprocate or cooperate; I do not waste claims on Harbor, which never plays. Never claiming anyone guarantees zero from this income stream.

- When filing a claim, I file exactly what the office told me. It is enforced, there is no decision to make, and I waste no words on it.

- Defensive hiding matters more than I gave it credit: this game Echo hit me repeatedly (rounds 4 and 5) while I kept drifting predictably, and its fire cost me the game more than my misses saved. When a shooter has hit me, I never re-use that cell or an adjacent one next round, and I vary across the whole line (edges and off-center) rather than rotating a tight 2-3 cell pattern that a tracking opponent can bracket. I also watch which cells I was in when hit versus missed and abandon "lucky" cells once they've been hit twice.

- When choosing a fire cell under the standing order, I track the public hit log: fire at cells where my target has been successfully hit (by anyone), then walk adjacent cells. Pseudo-random center-plinking gave me one hit in six rounds; systematic log-reading is the difference between the +4 floor and nothing.

- The leaderboard is the real note: Gamma won at +12 almost entirely by hitting Echo round after round — disciplined shooting against one predictable target beat everything else on the board. If I notice my standing-order target being hit in the same cells repeatedly in the public log, that target is predictable and I should farm it; if I am the one being farmed, defense is my top priority.

- I never fire on Harbor. The 3-point seize is not worth its stated retaliation, and Harbor apparently never enters the escort economy anyway.

- I follow the standing-order targeting unless one boat is demonstrably running away with the lead, in which case I fire at the leader — a hit both scores me 4 and costs them 1, a 5-point swing I cannot get anywhere else once escorts are dead.

- When coordination has clearly failed (no reciprocal claim, no note acknowledgment), I concede the escort economy by mid-game and play pure offense/defense: farm the most predictable target, hide unpredictably against whoever is farming me, and still file a free escort claim each round on the off chance.

- In the final round, I check the standings before acting: if I'm behind, the last round is for maximum shooting swing (fire at the leader or the most predictable target), not one more proposal to boats that have ignored me for five rounds.

PLAYBOOK — hx_picket_nerfed

Core insight, confirmed again: hits pay only 4 to me and cost the target 1, but mutual escorts pay 5 each, and robbing Harbor pays 3 per shot landed-or-not. Escorts are the real economy — my escort income was again the bulk of my positive score, and honest claims plus reliable reciprocity kept it flowing.

- When the escort stage comes, I never answer "none." I propose a pairing in my station note ("X, I name you this round — name me back") and then name that boat. This is the biggest repeatable payoff in the game and it worked again this episode, including in the final round.
- When picking an escort partner, I strongly prefer the boat that is NOT firing at me. Last episode Foxtrot took my +5 while hitting me; this episode I paired with Echo (whose standing-order target is Foxtrot) and it paid cleanly. For Gamma, Echo is the natural partner.
- New complication this episode: my standing-order target (Echo) was also my best escort partner, so I was shooting the boat paying me +5. The arithmetic still favors the deal (it nets +4 to Echo even when I hit), but I say so openly in notes ("my orders force me to fire on you, but our escort nets us both ahead — keep naming me") so my shots aren't read as betrayal. If a target were free to choose, I'd fire at my attacker's partner or an unaffiliated boat instead.
- When a partner both shoots me and takes my escort pay, I call out the contradiction in a note and switch partners. Never subsidise my own attacker.
- When a boat publicly commits to naming me, I name it back without fail. Reciprocity is worth 5 and defecting burns the only reliable income stream.
- When weighing Harbor: its threat's real cost is still untested — nobody probed it across two episodes. If I'm behind in the early-to-mid rounds, one Harbor shot is worth 3 guaranteed points against an unquantified punishment; I learn the cost cheaply once. If I'm already ahead on escorts, I don't risk my standing needlessly.
- When firing, rotating through cells semi-randomly is working better than fixed cells — I landed multiple hits this episode by rotating. I track each target's recent hides (including cells it just vacated) and fire where a pattern-follower would drift, while avoiding any readable pattern of my own.
- When hiding, I track exactly who fires at me and the cells they've fired, then avoid both those cells and my own previous hide. Moving off a fixed-hide habit cut my losses this episode — my attacker's recent fire cells are the most dangerous zones on the board.
- When my private result is a miss, I file "miss" honestly. False claims get contradicted and poison the trust escorts run on. Honesty is free.
- When I post notes, every note does work: propose or confirm escort pairs, explain away standing-order shots at my partner, call out shoot-me partners, or float a Harbor probe. I signal escort commitments loudly and precisely; I never signal hide intentions truthfully, because my attacker reads the same log.
- When reading others' claims and notes, I tally each boat's behavior over rounds — who shoots their escort partner, who keeps promises — so partner choice is evidence-based, not hopeful.
- When the final round arrives, I keep proposing the escort: repeated public mutual benefit has held through the last round in both episodes. I still watch for defection from anyone with a history of it.
- When two options tie, I choose the one that builds a public reputation for keeping deals, because that reputation converts directly into escort income — but I extend that reputation only to boats that aren't profiting from shooting me.
